title: Deferred navigation registered before the site is ignored, while the same registration after it demotes: false must (F5a vs F5b)
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts:279-296 (the climb only inspects siblings after the site); packages/adapter-angular/src/supersession.test.ts:80-86 (pins setTimeout after the navigation as may)
evidence: The fixture (scratch/supersession/fixtures.ts, same harness as supersession.test.ts) gives `go() { setTimeout(() => this.router.navigate(['/b'])); this.router.navigate(['/a']); }` a=must, and `go() { this.router.navigate(['/a']); setTimeout(() => this.router.navigate(['/b'])); }` a=may. Both timers are registered in the same synchronous run and fire at the same moment. Whether /a is still in flight then depends only on its pipeline: there is a forced async hop (router.mjs:4625-4627, `return Promise.resolve(t)`), and lazy component loading (router.mjs:4731), async guards and resolvers add further hops. A navigation that arrives while /a is in flight cancels it (switchMap at router.mjs:4572-4573, SupersededByNewNavigation at 4585/4792). HEAD gives must for both orders (scratch/supersession/fixtures-head.ts).
consequence: For a lazy target, or one behind an async guard or resolver, a callback registered earlier in the same handler (a timer, an HTTP subscribe, a store dispatch whose effect navigates later) cancels /a, yet /a is printed must. Claim 3.1 fails. The new test asserts the deferred-supersession premise in one syntactic order only, so the rule contradicts itself.
fix: Choose one stance and apply it to both orders. Either treat an opaque call or callback registration anywhere in the handler, before the site as well as after it, as able to supersede the site, or state that deferred interleavings are out of scope and drop setTimeout from the test at supersession.test.ts:80-86. In both cases, say in ch3 which one the rule does.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding is real: the rule depends on the order of the calls. supersededAt checks for a competing call only among the siblings after the site (packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts:287, `siblings.slice(siblings.indexOf(node) + 1)`). Statements before the site are checked only by interruption() (conditions.ts:356-357 calling 199-205), and that looks only for await, return, throw, break and continue. So a timer or subscribe callback registered before navigate(['/a']) can never demote it. One small fixture run (scratch/supersession/verify-f5.ts, same harness as supersession.test.ts) printed:
- eager and lazy F5a (setTimeout before): a=must
- eager and lazy F5b (setTimeout after): a=may
- S1 (svc.load().subscribe(() => navigate /b) before): a=must
- S2 (the same subscribe after): a=may

The runtime premise holds in Angular 18.2.14 router.mjs: switchMap cancels the navigation in flight (4572-4573, SupersededByNewNavigation at 4585/4792), there is a forced async hop (4625-4627), and loadComponent adds a chunk load (4729-4731). The thesis does not count the chunk fetch as a demotion; ch3-analysis.tex:183-185 says only that a failed load is a fault of the deployment. Take a guard-free lazy /a: a 0 ms timer, or an HTTP callback, registered before the navigation fires while the chunk is still loading. Its navigate(/b) then cancels /a, yet /a is printed must. That is a counterexample to Claim 3.1 (ch3:137) as worded.

Parts of the finding are overstated or wrong:
(1) Async guards and resolvers do not produce a false must. ch3:159-163 already demotes any edge whose navigation runs a guard or resolver. Only the lazy-target path (and any other unguarded async hop) is live.
(2) The WIP does not introduce the F5a hole. HEAD's narrower rule, which only checks a later navigation statement in the same block, also gives must for F5a. The WIP only made F5b conservative.
(3) The test does not strictly contradict itself. setTimeout is demoted as an opaque call (mayNavigate returns true for any call with no readable body, conditions.ts:244), and the test name at supersession.test.ts:80-86 says "opaque later effect". The asymmetry is conservative on one side and unsound on the other.
(4) No printed figure is affected. Across all six corpus maps (maps/wip), the only must edges witnessed in a .ts file are the 63 k8sdash edges cited at modules/web/src/chrome/component.ts:82 (goToCreateState), and nothing is registered before that navigate. diff.json shows HEAD and WIP give identical modalities.

So this is a latent soundness gap in Claim 3.1's wording. It is not major.

ASSUMPTION: with eager targets the whole router pipeline settles in microtasks before a 0 ms timer fires. If so, F5a is correct for eager targets and F5b is merely conservative.
verdict.checkedEvidence:

- supersession.test.ts:80-86 (setTimeout at line 83) pins the after-site case as may, under the name "opaque later effect".
- ch3-analysis.tex:137 states Claim 3.1. ch3:176 states the rule as "before a later navigation in the same block". ch3:159-163 says guards and resolvers demote. ch3:183-185 says the lazy chunk fetch is not counted.
- Angular router.mjs 18.2.14 (node_modules/.pnpm/@angular+router@18.2.14.../fesm2022/router.mjs) checked at 4572-4573, 4585, 4625-4627, 4729-4731 and 4785-4792.
- Ran one in-memory tsx fixture, /Users/kanetran29/personal/uigraph-work/wip-review/scratch/supersession/verify-f5.ts, against the working-tree extractor:
  - eager and lazy F5a: a=must
  - F5b: a=may
  - S1 subscribe before: a=must
  - S2 subscribe after: a=may
- In HEAD's conditions.ts, supersededAt (lines 221-246) only checks for a following navigation statement in the same block, so F5a was already must at HEAD.
- Corpus: maps/wip/*.db were scanned. The only .ts-witnessed must site is k8sdash modules/web/src/chrome/component.ts:82, with no earlier timer or subscribe registration. diff.json shows no modality changes.
verdict.betterFix:
The main fix is a scope statement. A code change alone cannot close this, because a timer from ngOnInit or a second user click during a lazy chunk load also cancels any must edge to a lazy target.

1. In ch3-analysis.tex, next to Claim 3.1 (line 137) and the rule list (line 176), state that must quantifies over one synchronous run of the handler. Supersession is judged only for navigations started in that run. A navigation that arrives from another task while the first is in flight is out of scope, whichever side of the site it was registered on. That covers a timer, a subscription callback, a promise continuation, another event, and a lazy chunk load or other async hop in the router.

2. Narrow the claim's wording, at ch3:183-185 or beside the claim, to say that a lazy target's load leaves a window in which such a navigation cancels it.

3. Keep setTimeout at supersession.test.ts:83, but justify it as an opaque call. Do not make it a deferred-supersession case. Add a test that pins the before-site order (setTimeout or subscribe before navigate gives must) as the documented out-of-scope behaviour, so both orders are asserted deliberately.

4. Optional code tightening, only if the stance should be conservative instead: in supersededAt, also scan the earlier siblings in the same block for an opaque call that is passed a function argument whose body mayNavigate. Demote to may in that case. Even then, keep the scope sentence from step 1 for cross-handler interleavings.

title: Calling contexts stop at any callback and ignore framework lifecycle order, so 'follow all known calling contexts' is not implemented (F3b, F3c, F6)
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts:247-256 (containingMember returns undefined at the first arrow/function expression that is not a property initializer, and for constructors and accessors); conditions.ts:297-305 (callers followed only through this.member() calls in the class)
evidence: Fixture results on the working tree: (F3a) `go(){nav a}` plus `ngOnInit(){ this.go(); nav b }` gives a=may, which is what the WIP test at supersession.test.ts:71-78 pins. (F3b) The same with `[0].forEach(() => this.go())` gives a=must b=must. (F3c) The same with `this.zone.run(() => this.go())` gives a=must b=must. (F6) `ngOnInit(){ nav a }` plus `ngAfterViewInit(){ nav b }` gives a=must b=must. forEach and NgZone.run invoke the callback synchronously. ngOnInit and ngAfterViewInit run in one synchronous change-detection pass, and /a cannot finish before the forced microtask hop (router.mjs:4625-4627). In all three cases /b is requested while /a is in flight. HEAD gives must in all four cases.
consequence: Two must edges leave one screen although the first navigation never occurs on any execution of ngOnInit. The comment at conditions.ts:298-299 promises that every calling context is followed, but a caller inside a synchronous callback and the framework's own hook order are both missed.
fix: When a caller sits inside a callback, climb past it to the enclosing member at least for callbacks passed to calls (staying conservative), rather than returning undefined. Model lifecycle order as calling contexts: a navigation in constructor or ngOnInit is superseded when any later hook in the same pass (ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterViewInit, ngDoCheck, and the rest) makes mayNavigate true. Add fixtures F3b, F3c and F6 as tests.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the mechanism. One part of the finding is slightly wrong, and the severity is overstated.

**1. Callbacks.** The climb in `after` stops at the first function boundary (conditions.ts:280, `if (Node.isFunctionLikeDeclaration(parent)) break`).
- For a caller written as `[0].forEach(() => this.go())`, the parent of `this.go()` is the arrow, so the loop exits before it reaches the `forEach` call or the statements after it in ngOnInit.
- `containingMember` (conditions.ts:247-256) returns undefined for that arrow: it is not a method, and it is not a property initializer.
- conditions.ts:297 (`if (!member) return false`) then reports that caller as not superseding.
- `go` is a template handler (`handlersOf`, conditions.ts:140-141; `memberCondition` at :161 returns null), so `/a` stays must.

The WIP's own test (supersession.test.ts:71-78, "does not let a safe calling context hide a competing navigation in another caller") pins F3a as may. Its comment at conditions.ts:298-299 says every known calling context is followed. A synchronous `forEach` or `zone.run` callback is a calling context written out in the class, and the code skips it. The skip is also in the unsafe direction: the same file treats an opaque later call as a possible navigation (`mayNavigate`, conditions.ts:241; test lines 80-86), but treats an unknown callback context as safe.

**2. Router timing.** In @angular/router 18.2.14, router.mjs:4573 cancels a running navigation through `switchMap`, and router.mjs:4625-4627 forces a `Promise.resolve` hop after NavigationStart. So `/a` cannot finish before a synchronously following `/b` starts, and `/b` cancels it.

**3. Lifecycle order (F6).** `handlersOf` makes every LIFECYCLE hook an independent handler (conditions.ts:20, 140-141). Nothing compares one hook with another. ngOnInit and ngAfterViewInit run in one synchronous first change-detection pass (ASSUMPTION, from Angular's lifecycle model; not traced in core source). On that basis the ngOnInit navigation never completes, yet it is must.

**What the finding gets wrong or overstates**
- **Constructors.** The clause about constructors does not hold. For `constructor(){ this.go(); nav b }`, the sibling walk at conditions.ts:285-287 sees `nav b` before the loop breaks at the constructor. Constructors also have no `this.x()` callers to follow. The accessor gap is real but contrived, and the caller search at :300-305 never matches property accesses anyway.
- **Not a regression.** HEAD's `supersededAt` (removed lines 221-228 of the diff) only checked later statements in the same block that are themselves navigation calls. So HEAD also gives must in all four cases. The WIP fixes F3a and leaves the rest.
- **No measured figure changes.** In both maps/head and maps/wip, the only TS-witnessed must navigation in the corpus is k8sdash src/chrome/component.ts:82 (`goToCreateState`, 63 must edges). Its only caller is the template (template.html:56), with no callback or lifecycle caller.
- **Severity.** These are genuine counterexamples to the universal Claim 3.1, and the code comment overclaims. But the triggers are contrived, the gaps predate the WIP, and the corpus is unaffected. That makes this minor, not major.
- **Thesis prose.** ch3-analysis.tex:176-177 claims supersession only "before a later navigation in the same block". The thesis therefore does not promise the calling-context rule. It also does not describe the rule the WIP implements.

verdict.betterFix:
**1. Climb past a callback in `after` (conditions.ts:279-296).**
- Today the loop breaks at every function boundary. Break only at a MethodDeclaration, ConstructorDeclaration, Get/SetAccessorDeclaration, FunctionDeclaration, or an arrow or function expression that initializes a class property.
- At any other ArrowFunction or FunctionExpression (a callback), set `completed = false; valueWaits = false` and keep climbing. The callback may run synchronously inside the call it is passed to, and nothing outside awaits it.
- The existing argument check at :289-291 then treats the opaque callee (`forEach`, `zone.run`, `subscribe`) as a possible navigation. That is the conservative side for must.
- Later siblings in the enclosing member are also examined.
- Apply the same change to `containingMember` (:247-256): skip such callbacks instead of returning undefined, so that callers of the enclosing member are still followed.
- A navigation written directly inside a callback is already may through `callCondition`'s 'in a callback', so for it only the reason label changes.

**2. Model the order of lifecycle hooks.** Right after `if (!member) return false` (:297), add:

```ts
const FIRST_PASS = ['ngOnChanges', 'ngOnInit', 'ngDoCheck', 'ngAfterContentInit', 'ngAfterContentChecked', 'ngAfterViewInit', 'ngAfterViewChecked']
const i = FIRST_PASS.indexOf(member.name)
if (i >= 0 && FIRST_PASS.slice(i + 1).some((h) => { const b = member.cls.getMethod(h)?.getBody(); return !!b && mayNavigate(b, member.cls) })) return true
```

- Apply this regardless of `memberWaits` and `completed`: Angular does not await a hook, so an awaited navigation in an async ngOnInit is still in flight when the later hooks run.
- Helpers called from a hook reach it through the existing caller recursion.
- A parent's ngAfterViewInit running after a child's ngOnInit is outside the reach of a single class. Name it as a limit in the thesis.

**3. Tests and prose.**
- Add F3b, F3b2, F3c, F3e and F6 to supersession.test.ts with a=may. Keep F6b and a template-only control at must.
- Change ch3-analysis.tex:176-177 to describe the rule the code applies: a later navigation that the same execution, a caller of the member, or a later lifecycle hook of the same component can start. Otherwise, state these cases as an explicit exception to Claim 3.1.
- No corpus figure should move: the only TS must site, k8sdash chrome/component.ts:82, has only a template caller. Confirm this with the existing maps diff after the change.

title: A helper is read from its declared initializer, and accessor effects are invisible: false must through reassigned or @Input callbacks and setters (F1, F1b, F2)
where: packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts:217-220 (calledMemberBody returns the property's initializer body); conditions.ts:226 ('a known helper with no such effect is safe'); conditions.ts:230-243 (mayNavigate treats only CallExpression and NewExpression as executing code)
evidence: Fixture results on the working tree. (F1) `onDone = () => {}`, `ngOnInit(){ this.onDone = () => this.router.navigate(['/b']) }`, `go(){ nav a; this.onDone(); }` gives a=must. (F1b) `@Input() onDone: () => void = () => {}` with `go(){ nav a; this.onDone(); }` gives a=must, although the parent binds whatever callback it likes. (F2) `set page(v){ this.router.navigate(['/b']) }` with `go(){ nav a; this.page = 2; }` gives a=must. HEAD gives the same. ASSUMPTION, not tested: a subclass that overrides a same-named helper is resolved to the base declaration in the same way.
consequence: The rule's stated principle, that an opaque effect is a barrier, is broken. A mutable property, and an @Input in particular, is not a known helper, and an assignment or read through an accessor executes code. In each case /a is cancelled synchronously and still printed must.
fix: Resolve a property-arrow helper only when the property is readonly, carries no @Input, and is assigned nowhere else in the class; otherwise treat the call as opaque. Treat a write to or read of a member declared with set or get as a call to that accessor's body, and as opaque when it cannot be resolved.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds against the working-tree code. I could not refute any part of it, but its impact is smaller than "major".

Code, in packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts on the working tree:
- **Initializer read as the helper's body (217-220).** `calledMemberBody` finds a `PropertyDeclaration` by name and returns `getInitializer().getBody()` when the initializer is an arrow or function expression. It does not check `readonly`, decorators (`@Input`), or other assignments to the property.
- **Opaque only when nothing resolves (235-241).** In `mayNavigate`, a call counts as opaque (`else if (!body) return true`) only when `calledMemberBody` returns undefined. A resolved initializer body such as `{}` therefore makes `this.onDone()` look safe.
- **Accessors never visited (230-243).** `mayNavigate` enters code only through `CallExpression` and `NewExpression`. A `BinaryExpression` assignment like `this.page = 2`, or a read like `this.page`, is walked as plain syntax, and the get or set accessor's body is never visited.
- **Same resolver in the argument check (290).** `supersededAt` also uses `calledMemberBody`, so that path inherits the gap.

Fixture: I ran one in-memory tsx script. It uses the same harness as `supersession.test.ts`.
- **F1** (the property is reassigned in `ngOnInit`): `{n_b: may, n_a: must}`.
- **F1b** (`@Input() onDone = () => {}`): `{n_a: must}`.
- **F2** (setter navigates): `{n_b: may, n_a: must}`.
- **F2b, my addition** (getter navigates, `const x = this.page`): `{n_a: must}`.
- **Controls:**
  - With no initializer (`@Input() onDone!: () => void`), `n_a` is `may`. This shows the false must comes entirely from reading the initializer.
  - An opaque call (`this.svc.finish()`) after the navigation gives `n_a` `may`.
  - Two consecutive navigations give `{a: may, b: must}`.

Under the thesis's own supersession model ("the router cancels the first when the second starts"), each case navigates synchronously after `/a`. So `/a` is printed must although it does not happen. That contradicts Claim 3.1 and the docstring's principle at 225-226. The exclusions ch3-analysis.tex:181-185 declares (synchronous exceptions, lazy-chunk failures) do not cover this case.

Why minor rather than major:
- **Not a regression.** HEAD's `supersededAt` only matched a following navigate-only statement, so HEAD gives must too.
- **No printed figure changes.** Across all six apps in the working-tree maps, exactly one must site is programmatic: k8sdash `src/chrome/component.ts:82` in `goToCreateState()`, which feeds 63 edges. Nothing follows the navigation there. Every other must edge is `ng.router-link`, and `diff.json` shows head and working-tree maps are identical.
- **The thesis hedges.** The added ch5 prose says the checks "do not constitute a proof of soundness". Still, this is an undeclared counterexample to the only soundness claim, and it is easy to construct.

The subclass-override part (a subclass overriding a same-named helper resolves to the base declaration) remains an ASSUMPTION. I did not test it.

1) In `calledMemberBody` (conditions.ts:219-220), resolve a property's arrow or function initializer only when all three hold; otherwise return undefined so that `mayNavigate` (line 241) and `supersededAt` (line 290) treat the call as opaque:

title: Thesis prose still describes the old 'same block' rule, which the new code replaces
where: thesis-handoff/thesis/ch3-analysis.tex:176-177 (unchanged by the diff; PDF text at wip-thesis.txt:1488)
evidence: The prose says a site is demoted 'before a later navigation in the same block that supersedes it'. The working-tree rule demotes on any later navigation that may happen, whether in an enclosing block (supersession.test.ts:45-49), a conditional arm (34-43), a same-class helper (51-59), a caller's continuation (71-78), a finally block (138-140) or a comma expression (142-146). It also demotes before an opaque call or a `new` (80-86) and when a callee receives the navigation as an argument (conditions.ts:288-292). The corpus scan (scratch/supersession/scan.ts) finds 144 of 1,200 sites whose verdict differs between the two rules.
consequence: The thesis's description of the demotion rule is not the rule the extractor runs. The described rule is also the unsound HEAD rule: `{ nav a } nav b` would be must under it. A reader who reimplements the rule from ch3 gets different modalities.
fix: Rewrite the sentence to state the new rule: a later possible navigation anywhere in the execution's continuation, including helpers, callers and finally blocks, with opaque calls and constructors as barriers and an await on the navigation's own promise as completion. State its known limits (findings 1 to 3).

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the core of this finding. The thesis describes the old same-block rule, but the working tree runs a different, wider one. Three points weaken it.

1. Nothing on the corpus changes. maps/diff.json shows identical modalities between HEAD and the working tree for all six apps (mod, plusMust and minusMust are empty). The finding says a reader who reimplements the rule from ch3 gets different modalities. That holds only for code outside the corpus, such as the supersession.test.ts fixtures. No figure the thesis prints changes.

2. I did not verify the "144 of 1,200" count (ASSUMPTION). Re-running scan.ts would parse every corpus file that calls navigate, which is outside the memory rules. No saved output of it exists under the scratch directory. scan.ts compares callCondition's reason strings, so a site where the reason only changes, for example from "under a branch" to "superseded", counts as a difference without changing its modality. The count does not measure modality changes.

3. The prose depends on whether the working tree is kept. If the uncommitted conditions.ts is discarded, the sentence matches HEAD more closely. HEAD's rule is narrower still: the later statement in the same block must itself be a plain navigation statement (navigatesOnly). If the change is kept, the sentence is wrong.

There is also a structural problem the finding does not mention. The phrase sits in a list introduced by "when it runs only on some executions of its own handler" (ch3:171). The new rule also demotes on a later navigation in a caller's continuation (supersession.test.ts:71-78). That is not a property of the navigation's own handler, so the new rule does not fit inside that list.

title: mayNavigate is exponential in the helper call DAG (no memoisation)
where: conditions.ts:236 (`new Set(visiting).add(body)` re-explores a shared helper on every path) and conditions.ts:300 (a full class scan for callers at every step of `after`)
evidence: scratch/supersession/cost.ts: a class with `go(){ nav a; this.n0(); }` where each n_i calls n_{i+1} twice and the last helper only increments a counter. One callCondition on the site takes: 10 members 9 ms, 14 members 58 ms, 18 members 1,091 ms, 20 members 4,586 ms, 22 members 19,575 ms. HEAD takes ≤0.8 ms throughout. Time grows about 4x per two members (2^k paths). On the corpus the total is small (bitwarden: 213 ms vs 26 ms at HEAD over 287 sites), and termination is guaranteed because the visiting set holds the current path.
consequence: A large component whose helpers share sub-helpers (for example several helpers each calling refresh() twice) can make extraction time blow up per navigation site. No corpus app is near that today.
fix: Memoise per member body. Whether a body may navigate does not depend on the path except through cycles, so compute it once per class by fixpoint (or cache the result with the in-progress member treated as false) and reuse it in `after` and in the callee rule.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. I read the code and timed one small fixture; my numbers match the reported ones.

**Downward blow-up in `mayNavigate`** (packages/adapter-angular/src/conditions.ts:236):
- The line is `if (body && !visiting.has(body) && mayNavigate(body, cls, new Set(visiting).add(body))) return true`.
- `visiting` is copied for each recursive call, so it only ever holds the current call path. A second `this.nX()` in the same body is not in the parent's set, so the callee is explored again. That gives T(k) = 2T(k-1).
- Nothing short-circuits, because the callee never navigates and `.some` at :243 stops only on true.

**Upward blow-up in `after`** (:272-305) works the same way:
- `next = new Set(visiting).add(site)` (:274) keeps only the path.
- :300 re-scans every CallExpression in the class at each step.

**HEAD is linear.** Its `supersededAt` (old :221-228, in `git diff`) only checked whether a later sibling statement was itself a direct navigate call (`navigatesOnly`). It never descended into helpers.

**Timing** (my run of scratch/supersession/v2/cost-small.ts, WIP vs HEAD):

| Members | WIP | HEAD |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 7.9 ms | 0.81 ms |
| 12 | 15.6 ms | 0.16 ms |
| 14 | 58.1 ms | 0.17 ms |
| 16 | 246 ms | 0.21 ms |
| 18 | 1,076 ms | 0.22 ms |

- That is about 4x per two members. HEAD stays at or below 0.81 ms, as the finding says.
- A straight chain with no diamond stays at about 0.2 ms, so the cost comes from shared sub-helpers, not from depth.
- Memory peaked at 266 MB RSS.

**`after` is also exponential, which the finding does not say.** It cites :300 only as a per-step class scan.
- Fixture v2/cost-up.ts: an awaited navigate in a0, with levels `async a_i(){ await this.a_{i-1}(); await this.b_{i-1}(); }` (same for b_i).
- Because the navigate is awaited, `completed` is set and the sibling check is skipped, so every upward caller path is followed.
- WIP: k=10 154 ms, k=12 714 ms, k=14 3,292 ms. HEAD: at most 3 ms.

**Effect on results and severity.**
- Results are identical in every case. The cost is time only, and the code always terminates because the path set cuts cycles. Minor is right.
- I did not re-check the corpus figure (bitwarden 213 vs 26 ms); a corpus map is not allowed under the memory limits. It is the finding's own measurement, unverified here.

**The suggested fix is half wrong.** Its fallback, "cache the result with the in-progress member treated as false", is unsound, and in the unsafe direction for Claim 3.1. Example:
- Class with `A(){ this.B(); this.D(); }`, `B(){ this.A(); }`, `D(){ this.router.navigate(...) }`.
- Exploring A visits B first. B sees A in progress, gets false, and B=false is cached. A then becomes true through D.
- Any later sibling `this.B()` reads the cached false. `mayNavigate` returns false, so `supersededAt` is false, and a navigation that B → A → D actually supersedes is kept as a must edge.
- That is a spurious must edge, which contradicts Claim 3.1. Only the fixpoint option is safe.

title: Supersession mutants are mislabelled or point the wrong way: 152 deletes all traversal, and 155, 157 and 158 add demotion instead of removing it
evidence: after() checks block-level siblings, which are ExpressionStatements. Under mutant 152 (conditions.ts:243 becomes `return false`), mayNavigate(ExpressionStatement) is false, so `this.router.navigate(a); this.router.navigate(b)` is no longer superseded. That is the same-block case mutant 24 already deletes, not 'later conditional syntax'. Mutants 155 (:281 `if (false)`), 157 (:294) and 158 (:231) remove exemptions, so they make 'superseded' fire more often: these are precision mutants, killed by the must expectations in supersession.test.ts:95-118. The header comment (:19-20) still says ids 151 to 158 'weaken' the reader, and the sweepRecord note (:93) speaks of 'Each demotion rule the thesis lists', while ch3-analysis.tex:176-177 describes only supersession by a later navigation in the same block.
consequence: \SweepMutants will count precision mutants as soundness evidence, and a kill of 152 shows nothing about a test of the conditional-arm traversal.
fix: Replace 152 with a mutant that stops traversal only at conditional nodes (if, ?:, &&/||/??, case clauses). Mark precision-direction mutants and report them separately. Update ch3:176-177 to the new rule.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute each part of the finding against the code, and every part holds.

1. Mutant 152 has the wrong label. In conditions.ts, mayNavigate (lines 230-244) has only three specific cases: line 231 returns false for function-like and class nodes, line 232 returns true for `new`, and lines 233-242 handle calls. Every other node reaches line 243, the generic child traversal. Mutant 152 (sweep-mutants.mjs:569-571) turns line 243 into `return false`.
   - In after() (lines 272-297), the siblings tested at block level are statements. For `go(){ this.router.navigate(a); this.router.navigate(b) }` the sibling is an ExpressionStatement. That node matches none of the specific cases, so under 152 mayNavigate returns false and the first navigation is no longer superseded.
   - So 152 removes supersession for later sibling statements of every kind, not only for later conditional syntax. In the same-block case it does what mutant 24 already does: line 179 makes supersededAt always false.
   - 152 does leave some checks in place: the callee-after-argument check at lines 290-292, a sibling that is itself a call (comma or argument lists), and opaque or `new` siblings that sit directly as expressions.
   - Many tests kill 152, not only the conditional-arm tests at supersession.test.ts:34-43. Examples are :45-49 (`{navigate(a);} navigate(b)`) and :51-59 (consecutive helpers). A kill of 152 therefore says nothing about whether the conditional-arm tests work.
   - Conditional traversal is not a separate rule in the code. It is a side effect of the generic traversal at line 243, so no single-line deletion can match the label.

2. Mutants 155, 157 and 158 push the other way. supersededAt returning true makes callCondition (line 326) return 'superseded by a later navigation', which demotes the edge.
   - 155 (:578-580, conditions.ts:281 becomes `if (false)`): `completed` and `memberWaits` never become true, so later siblings and caller continuations are always checked. Supersession fires more often.
   - 157 (:584-586, deletes conditions.ts:294): `memberWaits` is never set through a returned promise, so a caller's await never completes the navigation. Supersession fires more often.
   - 158 (:587-589, deletes conditions.ts:231): mayNavigate now enters stored callbacks and declarations. It can only return true more often, so supersession fires more often.
   - Each of these only adds demotions. A test with a `may` expectation cannot catch them; only a `must` expectation can. They map to these tests:
     - supersession.test.ts:95-103 (stored callback, expects must) catches 158.
     - :109-111 (`await navigate(a); this.svc.finish()`, expects must) catches 155.
     - :113-118 (awaited helper that returns or awaits the navigation, expects must) catches 157.
   - Mutants 151, 153, 154 and 156 do point the other way: they remove demotions, which is what the sweep is meant to test.

3. How the mutants are counted.
   - The note in sweepRecord (sweep-mutants.mjs:93) says "Each demotion rule the thesis lists deleted in turn".
   - sweep-to-latex.mjs:42-48 counts every mutant in \SweepMutants and treats any killed mutant as covered. It has no notion of a mutant's direction.
   - ch5-results.tex:1118-1120 says the sweep "measures whether the tests detect deletions of those rules" (the demotion rules).
   - So 155, 157 and 158 would be counted as deleted demotion rules when they are deleted exemptions.
   - The current \SweepMutants still comes from HEAD. sweep-to-latex.mjs:35-41 refuses to run until the sweep is re-run, so this problem only appears once the sweep is re-run on this mutant list.
   - The header at :19-20 says ids 151-158 "weaken" the completion rules. That wording is defensible but hides the direction.

4. ch3 does not match the new rule. At HEAD, supersededAt (lines 221-228) covered only a later statement in the same block that always navigates. ch3-analysis.tex:176-177 still says "before a later navigation in the same block that supersedes it". The diff never touches that line: there are no `supersed` hits in it. The working-tree code now demotes in four further cases:
   - a later navigation in any enclosing block (test :45-49)
   - in a branch arm (:34-43)
   - in a same-class helper or a caller's continuation (:51-78)
   - before any opaque call or constructor (:80-86)

Severity is minor. No printed figure changes yet, and the thesis says outright that the sweep is not a proof of soundness (ch5:1121-1122). Counting the mutants and labelling them correctly still matters for \SweepMutants and for ch3's list of demotion rules.

title: merge-sweeps' identity checks cover less than its note claims, and two of its refusals can never fire
evidence: srcTree is the git tree of packages/adapter-angular/src only. mutation-sweep.mjs rsyncs examples/sample-angular-app, which extract.test.ts:15 and :134 read, symlinks packages/core into the copy live, and checks dirtiness of `packages` alone (:52), not examples/ or pnpm-lock.yaml. merge-sweeps checks the lockfile pins at merge time (:65), not at the time each shard ran. The sha256 is computed by the merge from the bytes it is handed (:69-70), so the 'missing SHA-256' refusal (:28, tested at merge-sweeps.test.mjs:41) cannot fire from the CLI and certifies nothing about where a shard came from. The killedBy check (:41) is always met, because judge falls back to 'a test failed' (sweep-mutants.mjs:81), and judge counts a short run, such as a test file that failed to load, as a kill (harness.test.mjs:981). The new gate parses only (parseDiagnostics, harness.test.mjs:913-920), but the changelog calls it 'valid TypeScript'. I checked all 160 mutants with in-memory oxc (vite 8) and esbuild transforms (scratch/mutant-transform.mjs): none fails, so this is latent today.
consequence: Shards run at the same commit with different uncommitted fixtures, core state or lockfiles merge into a record whose note says every shard had 'the same adapter source tree and unmutated baseline'. The baseline comparison is a test-count string.
fix: Record and compare hashes of examples/sample-angular-app, packages/core and pnpm-lock.yaml in each shard, and refuse those dirty in mutation-sweep.mjs. Drop the self-computed hash check, and require a FAIL line naming a test rather than the fallback.

verdict.reasoning:
Most of the finding holds when checked against the code. One sub-claim is wrong: the one about packages/core. The problem is latent today, and most of it is inherited from mutation-sweep.mjs, which the diff does not touch.

Holds:
1. srcTree is only the git tree of packages/adapter-angular/src (provenance.mjs:52-58). merge-sweeps.mjs:26 compares only that, the short commit and (:27) the baseline summary string.
2. Fixtures are copied without a dirtiness check. mutation-sweep.mjs:64 rsyncs examples/sample-angular-app from the working tree, and extract.test.ts:15 and :134 read it. The checks at :52 and :98 cover only `packages`. So uncommitted fixture edits enter a shard unrecorded, and the merged note still says the sweep ran "at ${commit}" (merge-sweeps.mjs:50). The baseline check would not notice, since it compares a test-count string.
3. The lockfile is checked at the wrong time. pnpm-lock.yaml is never checked at sweep time, and node_modules is symlinked in live (:65). merge-sweeps.mjs:65 checks the pins when the merge runs, which says nothing about when each shard ran.
4. The SHA-256 refusal is dead from the CLI. The CLI computes sha256 itself from the bytes it reads (:69-70), and a hex digest always matches the regex at :28. The only other caller is the test at merge-sweeps.test.mjs:41. The check certifies nothing about where a shard came from.
5. The killedBy refusal never fires on a real record. judge (sweep-mutants.mjs:81) always sets a non-empty killedBy when survived is false, falling back to 'a test failed'. So :41 only rejects hand-edited records. judge also counts a short run as a kill (sweep-mutants.mjs:80; harness.test.mjs:981 `'Tests  379 passed (379)'` vs baseline 380 gives survived:false). That covers a test file that fails to load.

I did not re-run the finding's 160-mutant transform check. So "latent today" rests on its scratch/mutant-transform.mjs run, which I read but did not repeat.

title: diagnose-attribution now uses a different route set and shell to classify TabRemaining rows, and nothing records the change
evidence: HEAD called `collectRoutes(project)` and `attributeScopes(sfs, routes)` without projectDir. collect() skips root tables outside projectDir only when projectDir is given (routes.ts:1205), and shell election is unrestricted without it (attribute.ts:408, mayBeShell). The printed table was written with HEAD's diagnose, last changed in c0fe3b1, so its 'Owner component not reached from any screen' row (50) was judged against a route set and shell that differ from the extractor's. The 1.8.1 changelog does not mention the change. How much each application's count moves is an ASSUMPTION: it was not measured, because that needs corpus maps.
consequence: Row counts can move on regeneration with no recorded cause, and the printed figures came from a classifier that did not match the extractor.
fix: Name the change in the changelog, regenerate, and report the per-application change.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. Each factual premise holds when checked against the code and the files.

1. HEAD's diagnose-attribution.mjs:16-17 is `collectRoutes(project)` / `attributeScopes(project.getSourceFiles(), routes)`, with no projectDir. The working tree now passes `path.resolve(appDir)` to both and `'full'` to attributeScopes. The script last changed in c0fe3b1, which is an ancestor of eb9dab8.
2. The extractor passed projectDir to both calls at eb9dab8 (extract.ts:182 and :362) and still does at HEAD (extract.ts:190 and :615).
3. routes.ts:1205 skips a root table outside projectDir only when projectDir is given. attribute.ts:408 `mayBeShell` returns true for every file when projectDir is unset. The same guards exist at eb9dab8 (routes.ts:973, attribute.ts:215).
4. The printed TabRemaining comes from generated-before-after.tex:20-31. Its header (line 2) reads 'Extractor eb9dab80 ..., harness 1.8.0'. So the table was produced by the old diagnose, which ran with an unrestricted route set and unrestricted shell election.
5. The 1.8.1 changelog entry (corpus.json:4) does not mention diagnose-attribution, projectDir, or the renamed service row.

The divergence happens on the real corpus, not only in theory. I re-implemented workspaceTsPaths in node (scratch/wsdirs.mjs) to list which folders outside projectDir each app actually loads:
- **bitwarden:** loads apps/browser/src. That folder holds a root table (apps/browser/src/popup/app-routing.module.ts, RouterModule.forRoot) and an outlet holder that nothing references (apps/browser/src/popup/app.component.html). The old diagnose root-scanned the browser routes and could elect the browser AppComponent as shell; the extractor does neither.
- **realworld, k8sdash, mifos:** load nothing outside projectDir.
- **alfresco:** the outside folders (aca-shared, aca-playwright-shared) have no outlet and no route registration.
- **ghostfolio:** the one outside outlet, libs/ui page-tabs, is nested in route-component pages, so it is never a shell candidate. No route-shaped variable array was found in apps/api, libs/common or libs/ui.

So the classifier mismatch is confined to bitwarden.

Mitigating points, which lower the impact but do not refute the finding:
(a) HANDOFF.md:72-73 already records that generated-before-after.tex is stale (extractor eb9dab80) and must be regenerated. The movement on regeneration is therefore partly expected. It still cannot be split between the extractor change and the classifier change, because nothing records the classifier change.
(b) Every still-lost attribution owner in final7 (ctrl vs fin L.json) lies inside projectDir. The 'no scope' / 'scoped' split depends only on screensOf/shell/indirectShell, which come from nesting reach (attribute.ts:459-468, 473-503). A web owner flips only if a browser or library component nests it. That needs a selector collision. Four exist: app-root, app-vault, app-vault-header, credential-generator. nestingGraph narrows ambiguous selectors by direct import (attribute.ts:233-237). The two collisions that are lost owners (web vault.component and vault-header) are already scoped through the web vault route (vault-routing.module.ts:22). ASSUMPTION: bitwarden's actual row movement is probably small or zero. It was not measured, because measuring it needs a corpus-scale run, which the memory limits forbid.

A side note, separate from this finding: compare.mjs's DIAG key for the service row was renamed from 'service (not in this version)' to 'non-component source without a converted transition'. An archived diag.json such as final7/fin/raw/*.diag.json therefore prints that row as 0 under the working-tree compare.mjs. The changelog does not record this either.

title: The rewritten mutant list only applies to the uncommitted conditions.ts, and sweep-to-latex compares ids, not edits
evidence: Applying the working-tree list to HEAD's sources (scratch/cmp-mutants.mjs) leaves 151-158 unapplied, so keeping the harness changes without the conditions.ts rewrite breaks the anchor test again. Fifteen mutants were rewritten in place under the same ids, and 106 was inverted from 'catch-all redirect counted' to 'catch-all redirect never counted'. merge-sweeps checks each recorded edit, but sweep-to-latex.mjs:35-41 checks only id sets, so a full sweep recorded at the same adapter tree before a list edit would still be published.
consequence: The decision to keep or discard the uncommitted work cannot be split between harness and extractor. Gate strength differs between the merge path and the direct path.
fix: Decide on conditions.ts and the mutants 151-158 together. Have sweep-to-latex compare rule, file and edit per id, as mergeSweeps does.

verdict.reasoning:
Most of the finding's mechanics check out, but its consequences are overstated. Only one narrow, latent defect survives, and the uncommitted diff did not introduce it.

What holds:
(a) The working-tree list leaves 151-158 unapplied on HEAD's sources. These are the conditions.ts supersession mutants at sweep-mutants.mjs:566-589.
(b) Fifteen ids were rewritten in place: 46, 47, 79, 81, 105-113, 125 and 139.
(c) Mutant 106 was inverted.
(d) sweep-to-latex.mjs checks only srcTree (lines 15-22) and the id sets (lines 23-29), not each mutant's rule, file and edit. The finding cites lines 35-41, which only write the output.

What does not hold:
1. "Cannot be split between harness and extractor." Wrong. Only 151-158 depend on the conditions.ts rewrite. The 15 in-place rewrites and the new mutant 150 target HEAD's extract.ts, matcher.ts and routes.ts, which the diff does not touch. HEAD's own list already leaves those 15 unapplied on HEAD's sources (cmp-mutants output: "HEAD list unapplied at HEAD src: 46,47,79,81,105,...,139"). So the anchor test at harness.test.mjs:904 already fails at HEAD, and those rewrites fix it whether or not conditions.ts is kept.
2. The inversion of 106 is correct, not suspect. HEAD extract.ts:292 now reads `[...redirects].filter(([at, r]) => overlaps(path, at, r.prefix, every) && !metFirst(...))`, so catch-all redirects are counted. The old find string `!at.endsWith('*') && ` no longer exists in the source. The new mutant deletes the current behaviour, which is what a mutant should do.
3. "Gate strength differs between merge path and direct path." Misleading. mutation-sweep.mjs refuses to run when any mutant in the whole list is stale (lines 66-71) or when packages/ is dirty (lines 77-79). It records `what` from the list it ran with (line 116). So a single direct run cannot mix edits. mergeSweeps checks `what` (merge-sweeps.mjs:32) because shards come from separate runs. Both paths then go through the same sweep-to-latex.mjs, which has the same gap after recording.
4. None of the diff's edits can produce the claimed stale publication. Each in-place rewrite follows a source change, so any older sweep has a different srcTree and is refused at sweep-to-latex.mjs:20. The new ids 150-158 change the id set, which lines 23-29 catch. The only recorded sweep, results-must/mutation-sweep.json (commit a8c7480, 72 mutants, no srcTree), is refused anyway.

What remains is a latent gap in an unmodified file. Suppose a full sweep is recorded at committed tree T, and a mutant's find or replace is later edited in place while T and the ids stay the same. sweep-to-latex.mjs then publishes the old outcomes as if they belonged to the edited list. No such state exists now.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute the finding and could not. The denominator claim is false, and the WIP introduced it. The numerator wording conflicts with the thesis's own Chapter 4. Two sub-points need correcting, but neither changes the verdict.

1. Every printed conversion divides by all constructs, not the in-scope ones.
   - report-counts.mjs:27-29 divides CONVERTED_MUST by l.constructs.
   - l.constructs is the full parser count: loss-breakdown.mjs:347 writes constructs.length, and run-all.mjs:367 copies only constructs, lost and tally into results.json. inScope (loss-breakdown.mjs:324) is computed but never reaches results.json.
   - round2-to-latex.mjs:206-207 and :216-219 divide by r.l1.constructs too, so RoundTwoMustConv (1.5%) is over all constructs as well.
   - Printed values in HEAD's generated files, which the WIP does not touch:
     - realworld 12.5% = 5/40 (generated-tables.tex: TabLoss "Converted, must" rw 5, "All constructs" 40). In scope it would be 39 (TabRoundTwoAccounting), giving 12.8%.
     - bitwarden 12.9% = 17/132. In scope it would be 113, giving 15.0%.
     - TabBeforeAfter has the same issue: realworld after 30.0% = 12/40, not 12/39 = 30.8%; bitwarden after 10.6% = 14/132.
   - The WIP captions say "in-scope constructs" (ch5-results.tex:35-37, rendered at wip-thesis.txt:2652). Generated-round2.tex:20-29 defines "In scope" as constructs minus exclusions, so the caption contradicts the numbers.
   - HEAD's caption was accurate: "the fraction of constructs witnessed by a must edge (on this instrument, every construct a must edge cites)". The WIP made it wrong.

2. ch6:219-223 also regressed.
   - HEAD ch6:225-229 said the ratio divides by "all navigation constructs" and over-counts query-only calls.
   - The WIP says "in-scope" and that query-only, named-outlet and no-destination constructs "are excluded before the graph is consulted". The printed numbers include them: rw 1 query-only, bw 19 query-only, alf 7 named-outlet, gf 1 no-destination, all inside the 40/132/34/198 denominators.

3. ch5:877-879 is still false. It says the before/after columns are ratios over "the same \RoundTwoInScope{} sites" (1777), but they divide by 1820. This sentence was already at HEAD ch5:900-901 (prose-panel.json item 7) and the WIP leaves it in place.

4. The numerator wording contradicts Chapter 4, but it is close to the truth.
   - Unchanged ch4:107-110 says the round-two tables "count every construct a must edge cites". The WIP captions on those same tables say "own witness earns must" (ch5:36, 120-121, 220-221, 292, 307-308).
   - At eb9dab80, loss-breakdown credits each witness with its edge's modality (git show eb9dab8:loss-breakdown.mjs, the `rank[e.modality]` loop). Witnesses only got their own modality in 479cc6f/1ea65f3 (31 Oct).
   - Correction to the finding: 80d73e1 (29 Oct, before eb9dab8) made an edge take the weakest modality of the constructs that cite it. So every construct a must edge cited did earn must for that edge. The two definitions differ only in two cases:
     - a construct that earned must but was merged into an edge demoted to may;
     - the ±1-line crediting.
   - So the numerator wording is a definitional contradiction inside the thesis, not a large numeric error.

5. Correction to the finding: Section metrics is not silent on "in-scope". ch4:204-205, which is inside sec:metrics (lines 89-300) and unchanged, already says "over all in-scope constructs". So Chapter 4 contradicts itself: line 104 says "navigation constructs", line 205 says "in-scope". What is true is that Section metrics never lists the three exclusions or says they are "decided before the graph is consulted". ch4:231-232 and 263 say only that query-only is "not counted as a loss". "Names no destination" appears nowhere in ch4.

6. Related, separate issue: the WIP captions also say these tables were measured "on the final snapshot" (ch5:27, 37-38, 127, 217, 306). Their generated files are stamped "Extractor eb9dab80 ... run 2026-10-30".

Why major: the WIP replaced accurate descriptions of the metric with inaccurate ones in about six places, including the construct-validity threat in Chapter 6. The figures themselves shift by only 0.3 to 2.1 points.

title: '98.5% against 71.9% ... holds the extractor snapshot and in-scope population fixed' is false on both counts
where: ch5-results.tex:910-914; related ch5-results.tex:796-797 vs unchanged ch5-results.tex:853 and appendix-a.tex:87-91
evidence: round2-to-latex.mjs:230 computes \RoundTwoAccounted = (rec+dyn+unp)/tot.inScope over 1777 sites. round2-to-latex.mjs:232 computes \RoundTwoBefore = pc(tot.rec0, tot.raw0), and :97 sets raw0 += l0.constructs (all 1820) with rec0 = constructs - lost. So the denominators differ, and the predicate 'not lost' differs from 'recovered+dynamic+unplaced'. The snapshot is eb9dab80 (regen-round.sh:39-45: ctrl is the same commit without attribution; generated-round2.tex dated 2026-10-30), not final. WIP ch5:796 says round2nodes holds 'the final baseline and attributed runs', while that table's unchanged caption (ch5:853) says 'before and after the loss list was worked', and appendix-a.tex:87-91 says its denominator changed between oracles.
consequence: A 26.6-point gain is presented as a controlled comparison when the two figures use different denominators and different predicates. Two descriptions of Table round2nodes contradict each other in the same section.
fix: Drop 'in-scope population fixed' and 'final'. State both denominators (1820 vs 1777) and the eb9dab80 stamp, or compute the before figure over l0.inScope with the same predicate and regenerate. Reconcile the round2nodes caption with ch5:796.

verdict.reasoning:
The population half of the finding holds. The snapshot half is overstated. The numerical effect is small and runs against the thesis's own claim, which is why I rate it minor rather than major.

1) "In-scope population fixed" is false.
- round2-to-latex.mjs:97 (the same formula was at line 96 in 7d109c7, the commit that produced the committed generated-round2.tex) sets rec0 = l0.constructs - l0.lost and raw0 = l0.constructs.
- loss-breakdown.mjs:323-324,340 defines lost = inScope - recovered - accounted. So constructs - lost = excluded + recovered + accounted.
- \RoundTwoBefore (:232) is therefore computed over all sites (1820) and counts the excluded sites as successes. \RoundTwoAccounted (:230) is (rec+dyn+unp)/inScope over 1777.
- The denominators differ, and so do the predicates.
- Checked on the archived eb9dab80 run (final7.tgz, extracted to scratch/f7): the printed formula gives 71.5%; the same predicate over in-scope sites gives 70.9%.
- For the committed figures: 71.9% of 1820 means 511-512 ctrl losses. If the ctrl run also excluded 43 sites (ASSUMPTION: the committed run's files are lost), the consistent before figure is about 71.2%. That makes the gain about 27.3 points, not 26.6.
- So the sentence is false, but the mismatch understates the gain by about 0.7 points. It does not inflate it.

2) "Holds the extractor snapshot fixed" is not refuted.
- regen-round.sh:15-21 runs ctrl and fin at the same commit, with attribution off and on.
- In the archive, ctrl/results.json and fin/results.json carry the same extractor sha, eb9dab8030b0. The committed table also shows Before = 100% for every application, which is what a same-commit control produces.
- The false word is "final". The table comes from eb9dab80, earlier than the 0027017 snapshot that the WIP also calls "final" (HANDOFF.md:53,72-73). generated-round2.tex:2 records only "written 2026-10-30", with no extractor sha, which contradicts WIP ch5:791-792.

3) The contradiction in how Table round2nodes is described is real.
- WIP ch5:796 says the table holds the final baseline and attributed runs. Its unchanged caption (ch5:853) and appendix-a.tex:84 say "before and after the loss list was worked" / "before and after".
- The data (Before 100% everywhere, ctrl at the same commit) matches ch5:796. The caption and the appendix wording are stale.

The WIP relabels the row in compare.mjs:113 and diagnose-attribution.mjs:39 ('Non-component site, no converted edge') but did not regenerate, so the printed label is unchanged. ch6:63-64 says 'Each remaining loss is reported with the reason the implemented analysis could not place or resolve it', but generated-before-after.tex:135 prints 'Scope found, not explained ... 2' (also prose-panel #9, still open at unchanged ch5:322).
consequence: The sentence is false about the table it describes, and its own row label refutes it. The quantifier 'each ... with the reason' is contradicted by 2 unexplained losses.
fix: Regenerate TabRemaining at the final commit, or state that it predates the call graph. Say that \AttrRemainingUnexplained (2) remain without a reason.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. Only two details are wrong: the line numbers it gives for the generated file, and that it understates the problem.

1. The printed table is from before the call graph. generated-before-after.tex:2 records "Extractor eb9dab80". Lines 26 and 29 of that file print "In a service or guard (not implemented) & ... & 31" and "Scope found, not explained & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 2". The finding cites these as lines 132 and 135, but the file has only 61 lines. `git merge-base --is-ancestor eb9dab80 22dd294` succeeds, and 36 commits lie between eb9dab80 and 22dd294 ("feat: attribute a service navigation through a member-level call graph"). The working tree does not touch the generated file: `git status --short` on it is empty. HANDOFF.md:72-73 says so outright: "the round-two tables (generated-{tables,before-after,round2,plots}.tex) still come from extractor eb9dab80, before the call graph and the router-guard rule."

2. The new prose contradicts that table.
   - ch5-results.tex:330-331 (added in the WIP diff) says: "The final table records the reasons remaining after the implemented call graph, rather than losses measured before it was added." That is the reverse of the fact.
   - ch5-results.tex:328-329 is also new: "Some sites lie beyond the member-level call graph's supported receiver and provider forms." It explains the 31-row with a call graph that did not exist at the measured commit. This second false sentence is not in the finding.
   - The rendered PDF shows the contradiction on one page. wip-thesis.txt:3014 prints the "(not implemented)" row and wip-thesis.txt:3036-3037 prints the "after the implemented call graph" sentence.

3. The relabel was never applied to the table. compare.mjs:113 maps to "Non-component site, no converted edge" and diagnose-attribution.mjs:39 emits "non-component source without a converted transition". No table was regenerated after that change, so the printed label is still the old one.

4. The ch6 quantifier is false for 2 constructs. ch6-discussion.tex:63-64 says "Each remaining loss is reported with the reason the implemented analysis could not place or resolve it." Two of them sit in the row with key 'scoped; target resolves', which prints as "Scope found, not explained". For those, the analysis did place the site and did resolve the target, and no reason is given. prose-panel.json:147-159 (#9) raised the same issue for ch5:322 "Every one of the 170 ... carries a reason". That sentence is unchanged in the WIP, and no \AttrRemainingUnexplained macro exists.

5. The same overclaim goes beyond this finding. Table 5.8's caption, added in the WIP (ch5 diff, tab:recovery-source), says "on the final snapshot". \TabRecoverySource comes from the same eb9dab80 file.

title: Ground truth and ablation called 'final-snapshot'; the HEAD/WIP graph scores 100% recall, not the printed 97.3%
evidence: generated-groundtruth.tex:2 (stamp 0027017) prints full 183/5/0, \GTFullRecall 97.3%. I ran score-ground-truth.mjs on maps/head/realworld.db, whose edges equal maps/wip per maps/diff.json: 'full correct=188 missing=0 excess=0 precision=100.0% recall=100.0%'. round3.json [1] thesisProseToChange records the same change (183/5/0 to 188/0/0). Its corpusImpact also gives a final-code ablation: bitwarden full 167 sites / 1785 pairs vs printed 108/2284, ghostfolio 182/4097 vs 177/4087, realworld 39/188 vs 39/183. These ablation values are round3's record and were not re-measured here. Rendered abstract (wip-thesis.txt:67-70): 'recall rises from 94.7 % ... to 97.3 % for the full analysis', under 'The final extractor snapshot is measured'.
consequence: The headline scope-correctness figure attributed to the final extractor is not that extractor's figure.
fix: Regenerate generated-groundtruth.tex and generated-ablation.tex at the final commit, or label them 0027017 and remove 'final-snapshot' from ch5:344 and the abstract.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute the finding and could not. The working-tree prose calls the ground-truth and ablation figures "final-snapshot", but they were measured on older extractor code. The current code gives a different headline number.

1. **The label is new in the working tree.** HEAD's ch1, ch5 and thesis.tex never use the word "snapshot". The uncommitted diff adds it:
   - ch5-results.tex:344: "the final-snapshot ground-truth and ablation comparisons below are separate measurements"
   - thesis.tex:92 (abstract): "The final extractor snapshot is measured with attribution disabled and enabled."
   - thesis.tex:111-116: the abstract's ablation and ground-truth sentences then print \AblationFullAddedSites, \GTRootedRecall and \GTFullRecall.

2. **The printed figures come from older code.**
   - generated-groundtruth.tex:2 is stamped "Extractor 0027017" and prints full 183/5/0 with \GTFullRecall{97.3%} (line 44).
   - generated-ablation.tex:2 is stamped b5a9a44. `git log 0027017..b5a9a44 -- packages` is empty, so its extractor code is the same as 0027017.
   - HANDOFF.md:53 says these figures were generated at 0027017, "before fix rounds one to three".

3. **The current code scores 100% recall.** I ran the ground-truth scorer (score-ground-truth.mjs) once, read-only, on the HEAD and working-tree maps of realworld. Both gave `correct=188 missing=0 excess=0 precision=100.0% recall=100.0%`.

4. **The review archive already records this change.** In round3.json, entry [1] ("callgraph3") gives the ground truth as "before ... correct=183, missing=5 ... recall 97.3%; after: correct=188, missing=0". Its "Regenerate with remeasure.sh" list includes "generated-groundtruth.tex: realworld goes from 183/5/0 (97.3 %) to 188/0/0". Its corpusImpact ablation table gives full-level values of realworld 188/39, bitwarden 1785/167 and ghostfolio 4097/182 (pairs/sites). The thesis prints 39/183, 108/2284 and 177/4087 (sites/pairs). Only the realworld value is confirmed by my run (188 pairs, none excess). I did not re-measure bitwarden or ghostfolio, because the ablation script re-extracts the corpus, which the memory limits forbid.

5. **The rendered thesis shows the wrong figure.** wip-thesis.txt:69 reads "recall rises from 94.7 % ... to 97.3 % for the full analysis", under the abstract's "final extractor snapshot" sentence. Lines 3250 and 5091 repeat 97.3%.

6. **A hard-coded paragraph is also stale.** ch5-results.tex:554-558 says all \GTFullMissing missing pairs are on /profile/:username, "One cause, reportable as a defect". The current code no longer has that defect: round3 credits the recovery of those 5 pairs to the host-layout fix.

7. **No reading of "final snapshot" makes the label true.**
   - If it means the current code, ground truth and ablation are stale.
   - If it means the last measured snapshot, it still is not one snapshot. ch1-introduction.tex:164 claims the main tables are "regenerated from the same final extractor snapshot", yet generated-tables.tex and generated-before-after.tex are stamped eb9dab80 while the ground truth is 0027017.

The unchanged macro uses the finding cites are real: ch1-introduction.tex:198 and ch7-conclusion.tex:55 (the finding says 52-54). The final code's result is better than the printed one, so the thesis understates the result. It is still a false provenance claim in the abstract and the results chapter, and anyone reproducing the figures with the final code gets different numbers.

title: Rewritten abstract credits the call graph with \AblationFullAddedSites (35, 2.0%); its own contribution is \AblationCallGraphNetSites (6, 0.3%)
evidence: scope-ablation.mjs:243-245 computes \AblationFullAddedSites = full - outlet sites (1717-1682 = 35). scope-ablation.mjs:252-253: 'The call graph's own contribution is `full` against `class`, never against `outlet`: both keep the service join and the stand-ins'. ch5:465-469 confirms that full also carries the guard and effect stand-ins. generated-ablation.tex: \AblationCallGraphNetSites 6, \AblationCallGraphNetShare 0.3%. HANDOFF.md:128-129 lists this misuse as open, and the new abstract re-introduces it. ch6:78-79 says the call graph's 'marginal contribution is measured by withholding it'; withholding down to outlet also withholds the stand-ins and service join.
consequence: The abstract overstates the call graph's measured contribution about six-fold, attributing stand-in and service-join placements to it.
fix: Use '\AblationCallGraphNetSites{} (\AblationCallGraphNetShare{})' for the call graph. In ch6, say it is measured against the class-level join run beside the levels.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the core claim. The working-tree abstract credits the call graph alone with full minus outlet, and the harness says that difference covers more than the call graph.

1. The abstract reads "the member-level call graph adds \AblationFullAddedSites{} placed sites, \AblationFullAddedShare{} of the total, beyond the simpler levels" (thesis.tex:112-113). The PDF text renders it as "adds 35 placed sites, 2.0 % of the total" (wip-thesis.txt:67).

2. The macro is the wrong figure for that sentence:
   - scope-ablation.mjs:243-245 computes \Ablation{Full}AddedSites as sum(full) minus sum(outlet). generated-ablation.tex gives 1717 minus 1682 = 35.
   - scope-ablation.mjs:23-26 says full minus outlet is "what the service join, the call graph and the guard and effect stand-ins earn together". It says "only `full` minus `class` is the call graph's own contribution".
   - Lines 252-253 say the same. ch5:464-470 confirms that levels below full also leave out the stand-ins.
   - generated-ablation.tex gives \AblationClassSites 1711, \AblationCallGraphNetSites 6, \AblationCallGraphNetShare 0.3 %, AddedSites 6 and RemovedSites 0.
   - /Users/kanetran29/personal/uigraph-work/ablation/ablation.json gives class against full per application: realworld 39/39, alfresco 19/19, ghostfolio 177/177, k8sdash 62/62, bitwarden 106/108, mifos 1308/1312. That totals 1711/1717, a net of 6.
   - So 29 of the 35 sites are still placed when the call graph is withheld. The abstract overstates the call graph's own contribution about 5.8 times (35 against 6).

3. HANDOFF.md:128-129 lists this exact wording as open ("use `\AblationCallGraphNetSites`"). code-panel.json:381-389 records the same defect.

One part of the finding is wrong. The diff does not "re-introduce" the misuse; it keeps it. The HEAD abstract already had it at thesis.tex:129 ("places \AblationFullAddedSites{} more"). The rewrite moved the sentence without fixing it.

The same misuse also sits at ch5-results.tex:489-491 ("outlet descent adds \AblationOutletAddedSites{} sites and the call graph \AblationFullAddedSites{}"). The diff does not touch it; it is the HANDOFF item itself. That is the section ch6 points to.

The ch6 half is weaker but holds:
- ch6-discussion.tex:78-79 (new in the diff) says the call graph's "marginal contribution is measured by withholding it in Section~\ref{sec:res-ablation}".
- That section prints no call-graph-only figure. It gives \AblationClassSites (1711) next to \AblationFullSites (1717) without subtracting them, and gives \AblationFullAddedSites as the call graph's share.
- So a reader following ch6 reaches the 35-site figure, which withholds the service join and stand-ins too.
- ch6 prints no number itself, so it misleads only through ch5.

Severity: the qualitative message ("most attribution is supplied by mechanisms earlier work already has") survives. But the abstract states a false number for the thesis's own contribution, in the direction that flatters it. That makes this major.

1. thesis.tex:112-113: replace "the member-level call graph adds \AblationFullAddedSites{} placed sites, \AblationFullAddedShare{} of the total, beyond the simpler levels" with "the member-level call graph adds \AblationCallGraphNetSites{} placed sites, \AblationCallGraphNetShare{} of the total, beyond the class-level service join it refines; with that join and the guard and effect stand-ins, \AblationFullAddedSites{} (\AblationFullAddedShare{}) beyond outlet descent".

title: Table round2sound captioned 'Final-snapshot witness-check outcomes' prints a 20-edge tier with k8sdash n/a
evidence: Rendered (wip-thesis.txt:3675-3688) prints k8s dashboard 'n/a' (no must edge), All '20/20', Edges 11601, Judged 1857, Clean of judged 85.6%. The paragraph above it (ch5:932-933) cites '\MustWitnessUnread{} of \MustWitnessEdges{}' (62 of 150), and the final tier has \CensusMustKdash = 125 must edges. round3.json [2] corpusImpact records the witness check at HEAD: cited sites 16807 (printed 15752), judged 1456 (printed 1857), clean of judged 75.9% (printed 85.6%), ghostfolio 7/20 = 35.0% (printed 93.6%), with all 62 unread must edges in k8sdash. The caption says the must count 'includes unread destinations', but this table's must edges have none, and its column header still reads 'Must clean', because round2-to-latex.mjs:201 was changed without regeneration (likewise compare.mjs:97 for TabBeforeAfter, caption ch5:217-222).
consequence: A reader comparing the 'final' table with the 'final' text sees 20 must edges against 150, and site-level clean shares inflated by up to 58 points against the current checker.
fix: Regenerate with regen-round.sh at the final commit, or caption it as eb9dab80 / harness 1.8.0 and move the unread sentence to the 150-edge tier.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this finding and could not. The uncommitted diff (ch5 hunk @@ -942) changed the table's labels without changing its data. The old caption said honestly that the table was measured "before the fourth correction of this section, which keeps \MustFateKept{} of the tier's edges". The diff replaced it with "Final-snapshot witness-check outcomes and must conversion after the repairs" (ch5-results.tex:935-939). The lead-in now reads "reports the final snapshot's witness check" (ch5:930). The data in \TabRoundTwoSoundness was not touched. generated-round2.tex:1-2 still says "Round-two inputs from round2, written 2026-10-30", and HarnessVersion is 1.8.0. HANDOFF.md:72-73 says the round-two tables "still come from extractor eb9dab80, before the call graph and the router-guard rule. They must be regenerated."

The table prints realworld 9/9, bitwarden 10/10, mifos 1/1, k8s dashboard n/a, and All 20/20 (generated-round2.tex:50-58; wip-thesis.txt:3681-3687). Three sentences away, ch5:932-933 says the unread count is \MustWitnessUnread{} of \MustWitnessEdges{}, which is 62 of 150 (generated-must-witness.tex:3,5; rendered at wip-thesis.txt:3691). \CensusMustKdash is 125 (generated-census.tex:44). round3.json [2] corpusImpact gives mustUnread "k8sdash 62, others 0". So the unread count the caption sends the reader to concerns edges that are not in this table at all.

The caption claim "Unread destinations are counted separately in the text" does not hold for this table's own numbers. The witness-check.mjs at eb9dab8 has 0 occurrences of TARGET_UNREAD (git show eb9dab8:...witness-check.mjs | grep -c). eb9dab8 is an ancestor of 2b9802f, the commit that added unread reads. The checker that produced 20/20 had no unread verdict, so nothing in the text separates unread edges out of this table's 20.

The site-level figures match the old checker exactly, not the current one. The printed ghostfolio row is 202 judged, 93.6 %. round3.json [2] records the old checker on HEAD graphs giving 189/202 = 93.6 %, and the current checker giving 7/20 = 35.0 %: a 58.6-point gap caused entirely by the checker. Corpus totals: printed 15752 cited, 1857 judged, 85.6 %. round3 at HEAD with the new checker: 16807 cited, 1456 judged, 75.9 %.

The column header is also stale. round2-to-latex.mjs:201 was changed in the diff to "Must: no failure", but generated-round2.tex:49 still prints "Must\\clean". The PDF shows "Must clean" (wip-thesis.txt:3679) under a caption that avoids the word "clean". compare.mjs:97 is the same: changed to "Must: no failure" while generated-before-after.tex:6 and the PDF (wip-thesis.txt:2893) still print "Must-tier clean".

The diff also introduced a contradiction next to the TabBeforeAfter table. The caption at ch5:217 says "on the final evaluated snapshot", but generated-before-after.tex:2 says "Extractor eb9dab80 ... harness 1.8.0". ch5:235-236 says "The attributed run has \CensusMust{} (150) must edges against \CensusBaseMust{} (17)". The next paragraph, ch5:240-241, says "The final must tiers contain \AttrMustBefore{} (18) edges without attribution and \AttrMustAfter{} (20) with it" (rendered at wip-thesis.txt:2938 and 2941).

The pre-diff text was accurate about this provenance, so the uncommitted change makes the thesis less accurate. It is major, not critical: Claim 3.1's 150-edge tier itself is unaffected (diff.json shows the must edges identical between head and wip), but the table a reader is pointed to as the soundness evidence reports a different tier, measured with a different checker.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding holds. One detail is overstated, and the fix it proposes should go further.

1. The WIP's own prose. In ch5-results.tex:1118-1121 the WIP replaces HEAD's sentence. HEAD said "the rules themselves are each covered by a test that fails when the rule is deleted (\SweepMutants{} mutants ... at \SweepCommit; \SweepFirstPass{} were killed ... the \SweepAdded{} that survived ...)". The WIP version reads: "The implementation's demotion rules are also exercised by a mutation sweep (\SweepMutants{} mutants at \texttt{\SweepCommit})". That renders as "72 mutants at a8c7480" (wip-thesis.txt:3869). The sentence sits right after "\MustWitnessEdges{} final must edges". The thesis calls its figures the "final extractor snapshot" (wip-thesis.txt:50, 400, 3519). It never prints the commit of that final extractor: the only commits in the PDF text are f17a302 and a8c7480. So a reader cannot tell that a8c7480 is not the final code. The WIP also drops the macros \SweepFirstPass and \SweepAdded, so it no longer says that 6 of the 72 mutants survived the suite at the time.

2. The final code has changed since a8c7480, as the finding says.
- `git rev-list --count --no-merges a8c7480..469b210 -- packages` returns 8. Seven of those change non-test source: 56eccb8 (guards Angular runs), 758170f, ee54953 and 2e4090d (router follow-ups), 5350856, c8f956f and 2e2db82. They touch attribute.ts, extract.ts, routes.ts, callgraph.ts and matcher.ts, 2204 lines in all.
- The WIP's conditions.ts replaces `navigatesOnly` with `mayNavigate`, and `supersededAt` now follows helpers, conditional arms and calling contexts.
- The WIP's sweep-mutants.mjs exports 160 MUTANTS; HEAD's exports 151. The nine new ones are 150 (extract.ts) and 151-158 (conditions.ts, "supersession: ..."). mutation-sweep.json holds 72 mutants at a8c7480 and none of 150-158. So the WIP wrote mutants for its new rule and never ran them.
- HANDOFF.md:67 calls the sweep "Stale". HANDOFF.md:114-117 (Open work 3) says a full re-run is still needed and that a round-two triage found 28 survivors.
- The corpus.json 1.8.1 changelog says the list is "aligned with current router rules", but the macros still come from the old 72-mutant run.

3. Overstated parts. The finding counts "10 packages commits"; the real count is 8 non-merge (11 with merges). It also says a8c7480 "precedes 0027017", but `git diff --stat a8c7480 0027017 -- packages` changes only panel3.test.ts. So the sweep ran on the same extractor source as the must-tier figures the thesis prints. Relative to those printed numbers the sweep is consistent; it is stale only relative to the code that will ship. In addition, maps/diff.json shows identical edges and modalities between HEAD and WIP, so the claim's edge set is unchanged. None of this changes the defect: the sentence presents the sweep as testing "the implementation's" rules, and neither the router rules after 0027017 nor the WIP's supersession rule were ever swept.

4. A second statement the finding missed. ch3-analysis.tex:186-188 makes the same claim in the present tense and as a universal: "a mutation sweep deletes each rule in turn and checks that some test fails". The WIP leaves it as it was. It also leaves ch3:176-177 describing the old rule ("before a later navigation in the same block that supersedes it"), although conditions.ts now implements a broader one.

The severity is minor: the prose is hedged ("not whether the rules are a complete account", "not ... a proof"), the commit is printed, and the corpus edges do not change.

(1) Caption against row. Confirmed. The diff rewrote the witness row at ch5:174 to "Witness check, final attributed must tier". Its n is \MustWitnessEdges{}, which generated-must-witness.tex:3 sets to 150. 150 is the attributed must count (realworld 9 + k8sdash 125 + bitwarden 1 + mifos 15). The diff left untouched both the caption at ch5:166 ("..., baseline") and ch5:160-161 ("reports the witness check ... on this baseline"). Both still appear in the PDF (wip-thesis.txt:2838 and 2852). The finding numbers the table 5.4; the PDF numbers it 5.5. That error does not change the substance.

(2) Hand-compiled count. Mostly confirmed. The new ch4:542-544 says three items are "explicitly marked as compiled by hand": the defect-class summary, the oracle summary and the inspection of unreached components. ch5 marks only two: ch5:97 (tab:defects) and ch5:168 (tab:oracles). No table caption in ch5 or appendix-a marks an unreached-component inspection as hand-written. thesis.tex:150 still says "the two tables marked as compiled by hand". The three-item wording was already in HEAD at ch6:368-369 and ch7:108, so what the diff adds is the false claim "explicitly marked". The "two vs three" clash with thesis.tex:150 is softer, because the third item is not called a table.

(3) Probe terminology. Confirmed. The diff changes 'answered' to 'mounted' or 'enumerates' at thesis.tex:97, ch6:15-17 and ch7:137. ch5:824 still reads "\ProbeMissed{} answered addresses without a node". appendix-a.tex (the probe section, around lines 405-445) separates the two terms: a catch-all route answers every address, so an answered address is not evidence that anything is mounted there. The leftover word at ch5:824 is therefore a real mismatch, not a synonym.

(4) RQ3 criterion. Overstated.
- The decision rule was removed. HEAD ch4:279-280 read "RQ3 is answered positively only if coverage rises and must-tier precision does not fall". HEAD ch5:592 claimed that rule was met. The diff removes both and puts "RQ3 seeks greater coverage without a loss of must-tier precision" at ch4:286-289.
- But the precision requirement itself stays, as a goal ("seeks ... without a loss of must-tier precision").
- The text also states that the requirement is not established. ch5:573-576: "limited evidence for RQ3's precision requirement: unread edges do not pass". ch6 (wip-thesis.txt:4175-4181): "a measured recovery gain with limited correctness evidence, not a precision guarantee". ch7:53: "The results therefore do not establish precision for the whole tier."
- So the claim that the text never says the precision half is undetermined is false in substance. What is true is narrower: the pass/fail rule fixed before the results were known was weakened to a goal afterwards, and RQ3 gets no explicit verdict against it. Calling that "dropped rather than reported as not met" misstates the outcome. Under the rule the precision half is undetermined, not "not met".
